question: How does this ore become a salable product?
title: Mining and Mineral Processing: A Practical Reference
lede: Every metal in the other sheets starts as rock that is mostly not the metal. Getting from a 0.5% copper orebody to a cathode means moving, breaking, separating, and refining hundreds of tons of rock per ton of product, and most of the cost and nearly all of the environmental exposure sits in those steps. This guide catalogs {{N_ENTRIES}} processes across seven classes, with throughput, energy intensity, and water use.

facets.label: Commodity
facets.tip: Which commodities the process is normally used for. Base metals are copper, nickel, zinc, and lead · Battery metals covers lithium, cobalt, and graphite · Bulk means iron ore and coal, where scale dominates · Industrial minerals covers aggregates, potash, phosphate, and salt.

facets.label: Throughput
facets.tip: Material moved or treated per day at a typical operation using this process. Mining and processing economics are almost entirely about scale, and a method that cannot reach the throughput an orebody needs is the wrong method regardless of its recovery.

facets.label: Energy
facets.tip: Energy intensity relative to other steps in the same flowsheet. Comminution alone is roughly 3–4% of global electricity, so grinding is usually the single largest line on a mine's power bill, and smelting is the largest fuel line.

facets.label: Water use
facets.tip: Water consumed per ton treated, which is what decides whether a process can be used in an arid district. Flotation and hydrometallurgy are wet by nature; dry crushing, ore sorting, and filtered tailings exist largely to reduce this number.

facets.label: Maturity
facets.tip: Mature = standard practice for a century or more · Established = widely used and well understood · Emerging = commercial but still spreading · Early = pilots and first plants.
